title: Six Virtues on a Terrace: Kanazawa's Castle, Canals and Garden
standfirst: Between two rivers on a raised terrace, a fortified Buddhist hall grew into a castle, a castle drew water uphill through a hand-dug canal, and a retired schoolyard became a garden judged to combine six virtues at once. This dossier traces Kanazawa's castle town from a 1546 place name to the samurai lanes and teahouse street a visitor walks today.

paragraphs.text: The ground this district sits on is almost entirely river terrace and alluvial fan, built up where the Sai River and the Asano River, running roughly parallel, drop from the hills toward the Sea of Japan — the classic setting local histories describe as the terrace between the two rivers. The place name itself is first recorded in 1546, in a diary entry for the twenty-ninth day of the tenth month naming a "Kanazawa-bosha," a hall of that name; once the hall was gone, the name passed to the fortress and then the town that grew on its site. One well-known local legend explains it differently, tracing "Kanazawa" — literally "gold marsh" — to a stream on the Kodatsuno terrace where a humble digger remembered as Imohori Togoro is said to have washed gold from the gravel.

The fortress itself began as a temple stronghold. Kaga's Ikko-ikki, Buddhist militants, had already killed the province's military governor Togashi Masachika in 1488 and gone on to govern Kaga themselves for decades before Hongan-ji's tenth patriarch Shonyo founded a branch temple on what became the castle's inner citadel: Oyama Gobo, also called Kanazawa Mido, built from the start, in 1546, with the earthworks and timber palisade of a small castle. A succession of temple stewards held it for a little over three decades, until Oda Nobunaga's general Sakuma Morimasa seized it by force in 1580.

sections.heading: From a Militants' Fortress to a Daimyo's Castle

paragraphs.text: Morimasa's tenure lasted barely four years: he backed the losing side when Toyotomi Hideyoshi turned on Shibata Katsuie in 1583, was captured after the battle of Shizugatake, and lost the castle he had only just begun to fortify properly. Hideyoshi granted the district instead to Maeda Toshiie, who moved in from Nanao Castle on the Noto peninsula. An 1894 domain history remembers Toshiie as generous and broad-minded, a soldier who fought dozens of battles under Oda Nobunaga without a serious miscalculation, and a man frugal enough that he kept the same leather-wrapped sword hilt even after rising to senior court rank; when Nobunaga was killed in 1582 Toshiie wanted to avenge him at once but was held back by troubles closer to home, and later served under Hideyoshi instead. It was Toshiie's heir, Toshinaga, who began the castle's transformation in 1592 — quarrying stone from Mount Tomuro, digging the great moat still remembered as Hyakken-bori ("hundred-ken moat") to the south-east, laying underground pipes to bring water inside the walls, and giving the fortress the name it has kept since: Kanazawa Castle.

Successive lords kept building: an inner town-encircling moat by 1599, an outer one by 1610, and in 1631 a reorganization that made the Ninomaru the castle's functional center. The castle's main keep did not survive that century: built as a proper tenshu under Toshiie, it burned in a lightning strike in 1602, was rebuilt as a three-storey tower in its place, and burned again in a great fire of 1759 — after which it was never rebuilt at all, which is why Kanazawa Castle's skyline today is turrets and gates rather than the tall keep visitors expect from Himeji or Matsumoto. Fourteen generations of the Maeda family held the castle for 287 years, from Toshiie to the last lord, Yoshiyasu, who surrendered its lands to the new government in 1869; after the domain's abolition the army stationed a garrison, then an infantry regiment, then a full division headquarters on the grounds, demolishing what it no longer needed and losing the Ninomaru's remaining halls to a fire of its own in 1881.

sections.heading: Water for a Castle and Its Samurai

paragraphs.text: None of this worked without water carried uphill. The year after the 1631 reorganization, engineers drew water from the Sai River, raised it at Kodatsuno and channelled it into the castle's moats — the Tatsumi Canal, whose builder local tradition names as Itaya Heishiro, a man said to have died a violent death and to be enshrined, still, at a Hachiman shrine in what is now Kahoku district. A second, older waterway, the Ono-sho Canal, is more contested: town histories variously credit it to a Maeda retainer named Tominaga Sataro working in the 1570s–80s, or push its origin back to the 980s under a provincial governor, Togashi Tadayori, with Tominaga only improving an existing channel — even a 1995 study of the city's canals concludes plainly that no one now knows for certain.

Kanazawa's water engineering has a twentieth-century sequel. The city's own Furusato Ijinkan museum, which honors Kanazawa-born figures of note, records that the engineer Hatta Yoichi was born in the city's Imamachi district on 21 February 1886, and that he went on to design Taiwan's Chianan irrigation system and its Wushantou Dam, completed in 1930.

What is not contested is who lived where. Domain-era Kanazawa gave over most of Honda-machi, Nagamachi, Sansha and Hikoso-machi, along with large parts of several other districts, to samurai residences — by one contemporary reckoning, samurai land covered roughly three times the area given to merchants and townspeople. Nagamachi's canal-fed lanes and earthen-walled compounds are the clearest surviving trace of that division, and its mud walls still receive a distinctly local kind of winter care: woven straw mats, threaded with bamboo and tied to the roof beams and stone footings, to keep snow from grinding the clay away. Individual households did this on their own for perhaps two centuries; the city itself organized the work for the first time only in 1986, covering about 248 meters of wall, before extending the program to the whole of Nagamachi's remaining walls the following year. Not every former samurai residence stayed frozen in the Edo period: after the domain fell, one retainer, Abe Hekikai, built five pottery kilns on his own former residential land and gathered more than eighty workers trained in the old Kutani tradition to produce ware for export, a Meiji-era industrial reuse of samurai land that this district's local history treats as the start of Kanazawa's own Kutani-ware production.

The garden above the castle's southern approach went through as many changes of use as the castle itself. Its lower half, once a lotus pond, housed a Confucian scholar under Lord Toshinaga in the early 1600s and a construction office under Toshitsune later that century; Lord Tsunanori built a pavilion there in 1676. The higher ground had belonged to two senior retainer families until 1792, when Lord Harunaga built two schools for his retainers on the vacated site, with a dividing wall between the schools and the old lotus garden. It was only in 1822, when Lord Narinaga moved both schools elsewhere and tore the wall down to build himself a retirement villa on the enlarged grounds, that the statesman Matsudaira Sadanobu — invited, by tradition, to name the newly unified garden — reached for an eleventh-century Chinese essay on the gardens of Luoyang and chose Kenroku-en, "the garden that combines six [virtues]": spaciousness, seclusion, artifice, antiquity, water and a view. The domain's fall opened it to the public for the first time in 1874.

Much of what a visitor now walks past dates from exactly the transformations that history records: the Yugao-tei pavilion and its waterfall from Lord Narinaga's rebuilding; Kasumi-ga-ike pond, fed by a curving stream that is, again, water carried from the Sai River along the Tatsumi Canal; an ice-storage pit on the hill behind, dug to keep winter snow through the summer. Even the garden's trees were not exempt from the twentieth century's demands: a Hokuriku newspaper of 24 June 1945 recorded that Kenroku-en's own pine trees were being tapped for pine-root oil, a wartime substitute for aircraft fuel, in the war's last desperate months.

Kanazawa's teahouse district on the far bank of the Asano River carries a name younger than it looks. For most of the twentieth century, publications and residents alike called it by a plainer, older term — the "old eastern quarter" — a name that, by the 1980s, tourism promoters felt carried too much of the licensed pleasure district's old reputation. A new name, Higashi Chaya-gai, "the eastern teahouse street," began appearing in print around 1989 and had become the standard usage in guidebooks within two or three years, according to a 2010 newspaper account of the change. The wooden lattice-fronted teahouses themselves are older than their present name; only the marketing is a product of the district's late-twentieth-century reinvention as a destination rather than a trade.

Kanazawa's own good fortune in the summer of 1945 — a city that, unlike so many others of its size, ended the war with its castle town's streets essentially intact — is often noted and rarely explained in the sources available here; what can be said is that the city was still functioning normally enough in June of that year to be milling pine roots for fuel rather than clearing rubble. That survival is why the layers described above remain legible in the same few square kilometers: Nagamachi's mud walls and their winter straw coats, the Tatsumi Canal still running toward Kenroku-en exactly as it did in the seventeenth century, and a teahouse street whose buildings are Edo- and Meiji-era originals wearing a Heisei-era name.

Some traces are smaller and easy to miss: the absence of a tall central keep at the castle is itself a record of the 1759 fire that never got rebuilt, and behind Kenroku-en's ornamental stream lies a still-functioning stretch of a four-hundred-year-old water-supply canal, not merely a landscaped brook. The Hokuriku Shinkansen's extension to Kanazawa Station on 14 March 2015 changed how most visitors now arrive, but not the ground itself: the terrace between the two rivers, and the water led across it by hand centuries before any railway existed, still shape the walk from the station to the castle gate.

timeline.what: Ikko-ikki forces kill the Kaga governor Togashi Masachika and go on to govern Kaga themselves for decades.

The earliest written record of the name "Kanazawa" (a hall, Kanazawa-bosha) appears in a diary entry; Hongan-ji's tenth patriarch Shonyo founds the fortified branch temple Oyama Gobo on the future castle site the same year.
Oda Nobunaga's general Sakuma Morimasa seizes Oyama Gobo.
Maeda Toshiie is granted the district after Morimasa's capture at Shizugatake.
Maeda Toshinaga rebuilds the castle and renames it Kanazawa Castle.
The Tatsumi Canal begins carrying Sai River water into the castle's moats.
Lord Tsunanori builds a pavilion in the future Kenroku-en's lower garden.
Lord Harunaga builds the Meirindo and Keibukan schools on the garden's upper ground.
The schools move out; Matsudaira Sadanobu names the unified garden Kenroku-en.
The last Maeda lord, Yoshiyasu, surrenders the domain's lands; the castle is vacated.
Kenroku-en opens to the public for the first time.
A local newspaper records pine-root oil being extracted from Kenroku-en's pines for aircraft fuel.
The city organizes its first official straw-mat (komo-kake) protection of Nagamachi's mud walls, then extends it citywide in the district.
"Higashi Chaya-gai" replaces the older "old eastern quarter" as the district's public name.

caveats: Kanazawa's own Furusato Ijinkan museum confirms Hatta Yoichi was born in the city (Imamachi) in 1886; this dossier now states that link with that source.

The reasons Kanazawa avoided major air-raid damage in 1945 are not explained in any source read for this dossier; only the fact that the city and Kenroku-en were functioning normally as of June 1945 is used, not a specific reason for the city's escape.
The Hokuriku Shinkansen's 14 March 2015 extension to Kanazawa is now confirmed against JR West's own press release rather than stated as background knowledge.

Several internet-accessible NDL items that would likely deepen this dossier — an illustrated 1908 Kanazawa guide and the city's own 2010 academic study of the castle town among them — returned server errors from the NDL Lab API throughout this session and so are listed in furtherReading rather than cited as sources.
The Ono-sho Canal's date and builder are genuinely disputed among the local histories cited in S2; this dossier reports the dispute rather than choosing one account.

This dossier's 1923 local history (S1) gives three dates that a 2026 check against current official pages found do not match: it does not mention Oyama Gobo's 1546 founding at all, instead tracing the castle's origin to Hongan-ji's third patriarch Kakunyo and dating the 1580 capture to "roughly ninety years" after an undated founding (dropped here in favor of Ishikawa Prefecture's own Kanazawa Castle Park page); it dates the first tenshu's lightning-fire loss to Keicho 10 (1605) against the same official page's Keicho 7 (1602); and it dates Lord Harunaga's two schools to Kansei 3 (1791) against Kenroku-en's own official history, which gives Kansei 4 (1792). This dossier now follows the official pages on all three points.
